content: Deal Momentum Builds, Europe Stays Cautious

Global M&A momentum remains robust. Our Global Financials Team forecasts c.18% growth in global M&A volumes over the next 12 months. So far the recovery has been skewed towards mega-deals, as evidenced by a stronger rebound in aggregate deal value than in transaction count (Exhibit 1).

The H2 2026 pipeline is underpinned by structural supply from corporates. Portfolio simplification is accelerating, with divestitures supporting earnings visibility and capital reallocation towards strategic priorities, including AI. Survey data shows a record share of UK CFOs citing asset disposals as a top priority (Exhibit 3). In parallel, private equity faces increasing pressure to return capital, reinforcing reliance on M&A exits amid a still-fragile IPO backdrop (outside the US). With European IPO activity near historical lows, well-capitalised strategies are well positioned to capture assets at attractive valuations. Key risks include geopolitical uncertainty keeping rates elevated and concerns around private credit, which we view as overstated. European balance sheets remain resilient, with net debt to EBITDA below historical averages across corporates, financials and households.
European M&A remains subdued (Exhibit 2). The recovery
is lagging global trends, with Europe's share of global M&A declining to less than one-third of total activity, whether as acquirer, target or both.

Activity is increasingly driven by cross-border flows. In Europe, when deals occur, they are predominantly led by foreign buyers (Exhibit 4), reflecting valuation support and differentiated exposure. International acquirers are targeting European assets to capture discounts and access specific factor profiles, including Value and HALO segments, relative to the US.

Domestic buyers remain sidelined, reflecting weak local risk appetite. European corporates show limited acquisition appetite, consistent with equity flows where international inflows only offset persistent domestic outflows. This divergence extends to primary markets, with IPO activity still depressed in Europe. Survey data indicates that the share of CFOs prioritising expansion via acquisitions is near cycle lows, as focus shifts to cost discipline. Beneath the surface, take-private activity has moderated and sponsor activity, while recovering, is largely driven by exits rather than new deployment, as reflected in the Equity Research Sponsor Activity Barometer.

Discounted SMIDs and identified targets offer an exposure to an M&A upcycle (Exhibit 5). Our Tactical Research Team has rebalanced the European M&A target basket (GSTRACQN), comprising stocks with at least a 15% probability of acquisition. The basket targets both cyclical deal acceleration and structural consolidation, and trades at a material discount to the broader market (Exhibit 6).

Valuation dispersion reinforces the case for mid-market deal activity. SMIDs screen as potentially the most compelling targets given strategic fit and valuation dislocation, with STOXX Small caps trading on 13.5x P/E and at one of the deepest discounts to large caps on record (Exhibit 7). A broadening of M&A beyond mega-deals would act as a key catalyst, supported by improving bid intensity and rising strategic interest.

Broader beneficiaries are not pricing a sustained M&A upcycle, highlighting persistent scepticism in Europe. Investment Banking (GSSBBKIB), Holdings (GSSBHOLD) and Alternative Asset Managers (GSSBALTM) have underperformed year-to-date, down 4%, 5% and 15% respectively, signalling muted expectations for fee growth and capital deployment. This aligns with market leadership concentrated in select themes, with GSSBALTM among the weakest performers in 2026 alongside rate-sensitive sectors such as UK homebuilders, oil-sensitive segments such as airlines, and non-HALO exposures such as software.

Higher index targets. We roll forward and raise our STOXX Europe 600 targets to 640, 645 and 660 over 3, 6 and 12 months, implying 6% price return and 9% total return over the next 12 months (Exhibit 9), driven by the mechanical roll-forward since our Outlook and continued resilience in European EPS despite the war in the Middle East. We recently upgraded our EPS forecasts, supported by stronger nominal growth, AI-related capex lifting earnings in Technology, Utilities and Industrials, and higher energy prices boosting the Energy sector. With consensus revisions also turning more positive, year-to-date performance has been fully driven by EPS growth, while multiples modestly derated (Exhibit 8). However, similar upgrades across other regions limit relative upside, and we remain Underweight Europe, expecting weaker relative returns driven by soft domestic macro dynamics and more limited exposure to structural AI tailwinds.
